ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Urology Referral — Voltaire — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit for three weeks of visible blood in the urine and difficult urination at 83

text.paragraph: An 83-year-old man with three weeks of visible blood in the urine with small clots, a weak stream, and chronic retention (post-void residual 460 mL) with acute kidney injury, now drained by an indwelling catheter. Please evaluate the hematuria with cystoscopy, advise on the retention and the voiding trial, and interpret his PSA. [S]
Urgency: Soon, within one to two weeks; the bladder is drained and he is stable. [S]

list.item: What is the cause of the bleeding? Please perform cystoscopy and review the CT urography.
If a bladder tumor is found, what resection and staging do you advise, and what treatment options would suit a frail man of 83?
How should the retention be managed: how long should the catheter stay, and when and how should a trial without catheter be done?
How should his PSA of 6.4 ng/mL be interpreted, and is prostate MRI or biopsy warranted at his age?
Is it safe to manage the catheter and any clots at home, and what should prompt urgent return?

text.paragraph: Voltaire is an 83-year-old writer, thin (54.2 kg, BMI 18.8) and independent in self-care, who has had visible blood in the urine for three weeks, with small clots on several days, a weak stream, straining, and frequent small voids, and has been dribbling at night. He had been taking diphenhydramine 25 mg nightly for sleep and over-the-counter sodium phosphate enemas for lifelong constipation; both were stopped today. Six weeks ago he had a large nosebleed with blood also in his mouth after a coughing fit, treated with packing in urgent care. He has never smoked and has no occupational exposure to dyes or aromatic amines. Today: bladder scan 460 mL; a 16 Fr catheter drained 520 mL of pink urine. Urine microscopy shows more than 50 red cells per high-power field and 8 white cells; culture and cytology are pending. Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL; creatinine 1.68 mg/dL (eGFR 40), up from 1.1 a year ago; potassium 5.0 mmol/L. PSA 6.4 ng/mL, drawn before the catheter by shared decision. The prostate is enlarged, firm, and smooth without a discrete nodule. IPSS 22 before the catheter. He takes polyethylene glycol and started tamsulosin 0.4 mg today. Multiphasic CT urography with a chest CT is booked in two days. He wants to keep working on the play he is staging and to avoid long hospital stays [S]

list.item: Blood in the urine and difficulty passing water for three weeks; afraid it is something serious. [S]
Wants to finish the play he is staging and to keep writing, and does not want long stays in hospital. [S]
Has always taken many remedies of his own choosing and asks for something strong to make him sleep. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Voltaire, the pen name of François-Marie Arouet, was born in Paris; his birth certificate gives 21 November 1694, although he stated on several occasions that he was in fact born on 20 February. He was born into a wealthy bourgeois family; his putative father, François Arouet, became a receiver in the Cour des Comptes (the audit office), and he lost his mother when he was seven. He adopted the name Voltaire in 1718. [D]

He was imprisoned in the Bastille for nearly a year in 1717 after mocking the regent, and in May 1726, after a quarrel with the chevalier de Rohan, was beaten, taken to the Bastille, and conducted to Calais, whence he left for London. [D]

In a letter to the baron de Breteuil dated December 1723, he gave an account of the smallpox from which he was recovering: he fell ill on 4 November at Maisons; the disease declared itself after two days of fever with a slight eruption; the physician Gervasi had him take an emetic eight times and drink two hundred pints of lemonade, he had himself bled a second time on his own authority, and by the 15th he was out of danger. [D]

His biographer Jean Orieux, as summarized in a 1970 review in the Revue d'histoire de la pharmacie, describes a lifelong preoccupation with illness and remedies: he suffered from colic, took as many as eight purges and twelve enemas in a month, was persuaded he would die before forty, and really did suffer from his kidneys and bladder. In a letter of 1769 he wrote that being very ill was the common lot of old age, especially for one who had always had a feeble constitution. [D]

He returned to Paris on 10 February 1778, for the first time in 28 years, to direct rehearsals of his tragedy Irène; more than 300 people called on him the day after his arrival. On 30 March he went to the Académie amid acclamations and was crowned in his box at a performance of Irène. His deteriorating health did not permit his return to Ferney. [D]

His secretary Jean-Louis Wagnière recorded that on 25 February 1778, at a quarter past noon, while dictating from his bed, he coughed three times and said that he was spitting blood, and that blood then spurted from his mouth and nose. A declaration in his hand of 2 March 1778 states that he had been attacked for four days by a vomiting of blood, and the blood loss continued for several days. [D]

list.item: Visible blood in the urine for three weeks with clots, and a weak stream, straining, and frequent small voids, in a man of 83; under evaluation: active, confirmed [S]
Chronic urinary retention with overflow (post-void residual 460 mL at intake), worsened by a nightly anticholinergic sleep aid; drained by an indwelling catheter: active, confirmed [S]
Acute kidney injury from bladder outlet obstruction (creatinine 1.68 mg/dL, from 1.1 mg/dL a year earlier): active, confirmed [S]
Chronic constipation, lifelong by his account, with long use of laxatives and self-given enemas: active, confirmed [S]

Hematuria evaluation: urinalysis with microscopy, urine culture, urine cytology, blood count, kidney function, multiphasic CT urography with CT of the chest, and cystoscopy. Guideline: Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline (2020; amended 2025) (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, urologic cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia monographs (2026) [S]

Retention: indwelling catheter now, tamsulosin at bedtime, catheter care teaching, then a trial without catheter with a bladder scan; IPSS and post-void residual at each visit. Guideline: Management of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Attributed to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH): AUA Guideline Amendment 2023 (2023); Diagnosis, Prevention, and Treatment of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection in Adults: 2009 International Clinical Practice Guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (2009); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, urologic cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia monographs (2026) [S]

Medication review: stop the diphenhydramine sleep aid and the over-the-counter sodium phosphate enemas; keep polyethylene glycol; cut coffee to two cups a day, none after noon; sleep advice without sedatives. Guideline: American Geriatrics Society 2023 Updated AGS Beers Criteria for Potentially Inappropriate Medication Use in Older Adults (2023); Practical Assessment and Management of Vulnerabilities in Older Patients Receiving Chemotherapy: ASCO Guideline for Geriatric Oncology (2018) [S]

Shared decision on PSA testing: drawn before the catheter to interpret an enlarged, firm prostate, with the understanding that a raised value at 83 would lead to biopsy only if it would change treatment. Guideline: Management of Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms Attributed to Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH): AUA Guideline Amendment 2023 (2023); Prostate Cancer: Screening (2018) [S]
